utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. So this is Monday, June 18, 2007, and the Chamber would like to welcome the Prosecution, counsel for Defence, the accused, and everyone in the courtroom. So after what happened last week, we will now resume normally with the hearings, hoping that we won't run into new problems. We have a witness that's scheduled. This witness is scheduled for the entire week. Prosecution -- the Prosecution told us that it would need four hours and 30 minutes, and the Bench gave six hours to Defence, one hour for each accused unless they get organised differently. In the witness's written statement we found no trace that a special accused would be mentioned by name. It is quite a general statement, and this is why we're giving six hours altogether to Defence, and then it will be up to the counsels of Defence to split the six hours among themselves if they deem so. The Chamber also mentions that in the statement there are many elements that are not directly related to the indictment, and the Bench is asking Prosecution to really focus on items that are relevant to the indictment. So I think that's it for the witness to come. In the meanwhile, I also would like to give an oral decision regarding Prosecution's motion for extension of a deadline. Of course I need to find the right document. Now I have it. Oral decision granting an extension of deadline. We will require a private hearing, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Prosecution response to Defence exhibits tendered through Witness Bo Pellnas will become Exhibit IC 604. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, and now we can bring the witness into court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we do that, Your Honour, I have two matters. One very quick. Your Honours will notice that Ms. Alaburic is not in court today, but Your Honour shouldn't panic. She'll be back tomorrow. I've got Mr. Lasic and Ms. Juric as usual but it's my pleasure also to introduce another team member. I haven't got the courage to do it by description; I'll do it by location. The young lady in the far corner of the case Ms. Mackenna Mosier has joined our team for the next couple of months. Your Honour, the second matter is this: In light of the fact that for this particular witness, there was an indication by Mr. Scott last week that the Prosecution proposed to treat this witness as a combined 92 ter/viva voce witness, and following some of the discussion that took place in court last week, the Petkovic Defence and it is we who wrote -- we wrote to the Prosecution on Saturday, and I won't read the whole thing, Your Honour, because the absolute essential bit of it is that we ask that before this witness's evidence began the Prosecution should give us - and that's the Petkovic Defence but it would, we believe, apply by the same token, to the other Defences - clear written information as to A, what topics and points the Prosecution propose to cover exclusively or mainly by the witness's written statement, and B, what topics or points they propose to cover exclusively or mainly by viva voce evidence in chief. Your Honour, we made it clear that we would not then suggest that there would be rigidity, that they would be tied down to some inflexible demarcation by giving us that information, that simply wouldn't be fair. There's an element of quid pro quo or tit for tat in that. But, Your Honour, we do suggest that that is a fair request we've made. The current position is that we have not received an acknowledgement. So clearly, by definition, we've not received any actual substantive response. So simply asking, Your Honour, what the position is. Of course, what we had in mind - we didn't spell it out - we did indicate that it would be helpful, particularly helpful -- we said this, it would be particularly helpful if that information could be related, fairly closely and specifically, to numbered paragraphs in the witness's written statement and to the 65 ter summary. But, Your Honour, we tried to make it clear, we weren't prescribing how they should do it. We would like the information; the precise form of presentation, of course, is for the Prosecution. But to receive nothing, we do submit, is not a suitable and helpful course for this mixed procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you, Mr. Stewart. The Chamber first is welcoming your new colleague, and best wishes for your team. Now, Mr. Scott, I am turning to you. Mr. Stewart has been telling us that he sent you a written letter requiring some information on how you are going to proceed with this witness. Mr. Stewart is -- his request is similar to ours, because very soon the Bench will make a decision on how to actually proceed in this Chamber when implementing Rule 92 ter. So, Mr. Scott, why don't you answer Mr. Stewart? I believe that you should have done this at least out of courtesy. And secondly, how are you going to deal with this witness? Is it going to be a viva voce witness, a 92 ter? Are you going to combine both approaches? We know nothing up to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, and Your Honours, and everyone in the courtroom. Your Honours, we announced last week, the witness that the Prosecution is presenting this week will be a mixed 92 ter/viva voce witness. I wouldn't go so far as to really call it a 92 ter witness because the statement will be used, but it will in fact -- there will be, in fact, supplementation based upon some viva voce questions and a number of exhibits. So our position remains the same as announced in court, I believe last Tuesday if I'm not mistaken, so that hasn't changed. Your Honour, with respect to Mr. Stewart, unfortunately I did not receive the communications until this morning and I did look at them late this morning. We did not finish talking to the witness until about 12.00 today, so I did not have the opportunity to prepare any sort of a selection of paragraphs before coming into the courtroom. I would respond further, Your Honour, make a couple of points. It -- the 92 ter procedure may vary substantially from witness to witness based upon the nature of the statement and the nature of the material. It may be -- there may be some statements and some witnesses who can be -- it can be very clean to say we're talking only about this paragraph and this paragraph and this paragraph. There maybe other witnesses and statements, where the statement is such and the topics are such that there are a number of things mixed in from paragraph to paragraph, and you may indeed have a long paragraph with 12 -- you know, 12 or 15 sentences and we may take out and seek to clarify something in that paragraph but not other things. So if I were to say, we're going to talk about paragraph 15 but only one sentence out of 15, it could mean that. If I don't say we're going to talk about paragraph 15, then inevitably someone will say, well, you didn't say you were going to talk about paragraph 15. So with all respect, Your Honour, it's not -- it's not that clean of an exercise in many instances to simply say it's going to be paragraph 7, 20, and 28. So we understand the request that's being made. There may be times when we can be -- give a more abbreviated form, but I know in respect of today's witness, Your Honour, there are a number of questions spread throughout the statement that need clarification or there may be an exhibit on a particular paragraph that we -- that attaches to that paragraph. So it's not particularly helpful in this particular situation to say only this paragraph and only that paragraph, Your Honour, and so those where we are. But with respect to Mr. Stewart, I did receive that this morning, Your Honour. For whatever -- I didn't get the fax on the weekend, and as I said, finished with the witness at noon. We simply have had no opportunity to prepare any further response in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that simply isn't good enough. The -- on the first point of the receipt of the material, as it happens through a piece of minor confusion on our sides. We actually sent the communication twice, once by fax and I sent it by e-mail to the case manager on the Prosecution's side. We've received a series of the usual,, perfectly helpful letters updating us on exhibit lists, charts, and so on. The Pre-Trial Chamber will be entitled to be extremely dissatisfied, and so would the Prosecution, if the Defence said that we hadn't actually looked at these things because they hadn't actually got to counsel until sometime late this morning. We hesitate to criticise our hard-working colleagues on the other side of the case, but, Your Honour, we do say that the excuse that materials sent to the Prosecution team, actually twice in exactly the same terms, I can at least say that, on Saturday, for it not to have got to the -- to the lead counsel on the Prosecution side until just before we start in court or late in the morning. It just isn't good enough. They need to get their act together to make sure they look at this stuff. Turning to the substance of the matter, what Mr. Scott says in fact reinforces my argument. It's precisely because it's unclear whether this witness will be dealt with by this particular mix, whether that witness will be dealt with by that other particular mix. That's precisely why we need to know. The request on Saturday was for this witness and what we wanted was the indication in relation to this witness. The indications in relation to another witness may be different and, Your Honour, I didn't burden the Court with the whole of our not-very-long letter, but our last paragraph said: "We do understand that it is not possible to lay down rigid demarcations on these matters before the witness has even started her evidence, and that the more specific the information given by you in response to our request, the more you should be entitled in fairness to some reasonable flexibility as the evidence proceeds. However, it is important that we do receive this information from you." Your Honour, we were bending over backwards to be fair and to recognise that it simply wouldn't be right if we were then to turn round to try and hit the Prosecution, if they had been helpful to us, by saying, Ah, well you said this and now you can't do that. We were recognising the inherent untidiness of this exercise and the inherent need for flexibility but for us to know where we -- we are. Your Honour, we don't withdraw this request at all. We do say that the explanations, both as to what's actually happened by way of communication, and the substance, are highly unsatisfactory. It's not good enough. We really do need and are entitled to have a stronger indication about what we are about to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish whole-heartedly to join in the position expressed by my colleague, but I'd like to add one more thing. Perhaps an area where my learned friend didn't expound the issue fully. The Prosecution, a moment ago in the arguments put forward, uttered two sentences which were completely contradictory. The first thing that was stated was the witness would be a mixed 92 ter and viva voce witness, and then in the very next sentence, and that was on page 4, line 24, the Prosecutor went on to say that they wouldn't go as far as calling the witness a 92 ter witness. Now, why I'm on my feet is the following: First of all, I am not clear on this position, whether it's going to be a 92 ter or not. That's the first point. And secondly I'd like to remind the Trial Chamber that the Defence ultimately has to structure its cross-examination accordingly, bearing in mind whether the witness statement will be attended or not, because if there is -- there are allegations in the witness statement, and we know that the statement will be tendered or admitted into evidence or could be admitted as an exhibit, then we might have to challenge the witness on what he said there. Now, if the statement is not going to be tendered and the witness is testifying about something or not testifying about something, then we have to make the decision, to decide what portion we're going to cross-examine on and what portion we're not going to cross-examine on. And I fear that with a mixed approach or flexible approach, as the Prosecution I think put it, we would in fact create -- or, rather, it was in fact created to make the situation rather blurred, not clear enough, so that the Defence doesn't focus on essential issues, to blur the issue. So we must know. We must be prepared in advance to know what parts to challenge, and then we're not interested in what the witness says in testimony here. So it's a little disconcerting for the Defence, and it is difficult for the Defence to prepare with this system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, according to what I understood, I think this is basically going to be a viva voce witness and possibly supplemented by a few paragraphs according to Rule 92 ter. Is this it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure. I'm getting a bit confused frankly myself based on some of discussion. Whether it's a viva voce witness with a little bit of 92 ter or 92 witness with some viva voce, it is a mixed witness, that's what we said last Tuesday, almost a week ago. That has not changed. The Chamber has known, what we have done in the past in this situation is to tender the witness's statement, lay the foundation for the statement and then ask additional questions to the witness in terms of some parts of the statement, or about exhibits related to topics covered in the statement. Now, whether someone wants to say it's 60 per cent 92 ter, and 40 per cent viva voce, or 35 per cent/65 percent. I'm not sure how helpful that is. It is a mixed procedure which we tender the statement of the witness in order to gain the efficiency of time so as not to cover all aspects of the statement. And then to build on that statement with clarification, with follow-up, with exhibits, and that's what we are seeking to do, Your Honour. And in terms of what -- some other comments that have been made and Mr. Kovacic's question, what I've heard the Defence say, and I'm not picking any particular fight with them on this, I'm just simply recounting what I understand their position to have been in the past, is that based on the nature of the procedure, since the statement is tendered in its entirety, they have to cross-examine, excuse me, on the statement. Therefore, if that's the case and that's fair enough, I think that is the case, then it really doesn't matter all that much, we respectfully submit, whether we say that particular paragraph is handled in writing or that particular paragraph is handled viva voce, because the Prosecution's position is: The entire evidence is coming in and I've -- as I've said I've heard defence counsel say a number of times that in this situation, they may have to cross-examine on the entire statement whether or not we've approached -- dealt with it specifically, viva voce or not. So it really doesn't change anything, with the greatest respect, on that point. I -- my -- in response to Mr. Stewart, I can simply repeat, Your Honour, I -- I did not and unless -- unless Mr. Stewart's prepared to call me a liar and I don't think he is, I did not see that -- any request or communication until later this morning. I'll say it again. I finished with the witness at 12.00 noon today. I did not have time to prepare any further documentation in this respect. And thirdly, thirdly, as I said at the outset, the particular nature of this evidence, this statement, and this witness does not particularly lend itself to a -- to cleanly indicating only this paragraph but not that paragraph. For all those reasons, I was not able to prepare any sort of response, or at least it wouldn't have been a meaningful -- particularly meaningful response to Mr. Stewart, in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I've ever called a professional colleague a liar in court in about 35 years but I can assure Your Honours, the traditions of the English Bar would be such that if it ever does happen, which I doubt, I will say in such unequivocal terms that no one need have any doubt whatever. Of course I'm not suggesting that Mr. Scott saw the letter before he says he saw it. My criticism was something entirely different as to why it was that it hadn't got to Mr. Scott. So he can rest assured, it's not the first time he seems to be nervous that I might be making such an allegation against him. I've always been a million miles from that, Your Honour, and I am now. Otherwise, Your Honour, he is right. Where I do agree with him is 60 per cent this, 30 per cent, 40 per cent that, that wouldn't be helpful at all is the answer to his question. Because it wasn't what we were asking for. The -- just very briefly, it is important, for example, for the Defence to know whether in relation to a particular point, it is just what is in the statement which is going to be the evidence. In which case we can prepare our cross-examination on the basis do we need then to challenge that? Are we happy with what it says in the statement or do we challenge that? If we know that there may be more added on to what's in the statement, then it's more like a 65 ter summary, where we have to guard against the possibilities that may then emerge, and the different strands that may emerge from that basis. That's precisely, I'll be repeating myself if I go on any longer, that's precisely why we need this better information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you. As I said, the Chamber last week decided to give a decision regarding Rule 92 ter in order to make things more obvious, and obviously we must give advice very quickly in this regard. Now, regarding the witness to come, the Chamber believes that since the written statement has already been disclosed to Defence, this written statement is 121 paragraphs long, and we believe that -- that Defence must know that if it was a viva voce witness it would have to counter-examine the witness on the 121 paragraphs. If it's a 92 ter witness, then the cross will be on the paragraphs in the statement. So any lawyer after having read the written statement must be able to cross-examine. While you were speaking, actually, I was leafing through this written statement, and as far as I'm concerned I would have had no problem asking questions on a few relevant paragraphs. I'm saying a few relevant paragraphs, not 121 of them, because some are totally relevant. So this is how we're going to proceed. We're going to ask the witness to come into the courtroom. The witness will make the solemn declaration. The Prosecution will ask whether -- ask new questions about what is in the paragraphs. He would answer similarly as in the statement subject to some corrections and then out of the -- out of the statement and the exhibits in the binder, the Prosecutor will have four hours for the in chief, and we will render a decision in the days to come regarding new guidance because we already wasted 30 minutes since this hearing started for this matter, and I would rather, you know, spend 30 minutes on substance than 30 minutes on procedure, because the judgement will be a judgement on substance and not on procedure. I will now ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom so the witness could make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While that is happening, I just want to make one brief observation, Your Honours, and Mr. President. I've hesitated to speak up today, but when you give the Prosecution four hours and you give the Defence six hours, and then you allow this whole statement to come in, that's where it complicates matters at times for the Defence and that was the whole purpose of asking for some guidance. I just put that out so you might understand the predicament that we're in because, as a viva voce witness, I think they could accomplish all they want to accomplish in four hours, maybe five hours, but now they're having their cake and they're eating it too. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I fully -- I agree with you, Mr. Karnavas, and this is why we will soon make a decision regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. First I would like to know whether you can hear in your own language what I'm saying. If so, could you please say that you understand what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can hear you properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please stand up and read the solemn declaration. Before reading the sentence that is on the cardboard, for the record could you please give me your name, surname, and birth-date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Azra Krajsek. I was born on the 6th of April, 1955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a job as of now or an occupation? If so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am the founder of a company dealing with auditing, and I'm also an active auditor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you. Have you already testified in front of an international tribunal or an national court regarding the events that occurred in your country, or is this the first time that you come to give testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please now read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you may sit down. Just a few instructions on the procedure for your hearing this week. First, you will answer questions put to you by the Prosecution. I'm sure you have already met the Prosecutor, probably this morning or maybe yesterday. The Prosecutor is going to ask questions, and you will answer them, and the Prosecutor will also show you a number of exhibits, number of documents that you probably have already seen with him. Please when you answer the questions, be very focused and very brief in order to really answer the question and only the question. And after that step, which is going to be quite lengthy, counsels for the Defence on your left, and there's many of them as you see, but don't worry, they won't all be asking questions, there is one counsel for each accused that will put questions to you in the cross-examination. And if need be, the accused which are at the back of the room may take the floor also to ask questions to you also. And there again, please try to be very specific in your answers. Generally speaking, when counsels for Defence cross-examine, ask questions for the cross-examination, sometimes you can just answer by yes, no, I don't know, and you don't really need to go into detail. This all depends on the nature of the question asked. Now, the four Judges on the Bench may ask questions at any time and the Rules of Procedure allow for this. For a number of reasons we decided that we would only ask questions at the very end of the in chief and the cross-examination, but maybe sometimes when there's a document on screen, if it's a lengthy document with a number of pages and so on, in order to make sure that we don't waste time we might ask questions directly. It's a case-by-case procedure or system. But generally speaking, we would rather let the Prosecution do the in chief before we ask questions, and the same for counsel for the Defence. If at any time, you don't understand the question, ask for the question to be reformulated. Sometimes questions can be complicated, and then you have to ask the person asking the question to break down the question into different steps. We have breaks every hour and a half so you can rest and also so we can change the audiotapes. If at any time you feel ill at ease, you feel uncomfortable and you want the proceedings to be stopped, please say so and the hearing will be suspended. So this is how the hearing will proceed, and I'm sure it will proceed extremely smoothly. Mr. Scott, this being said, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Once again, thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, as is the practice with a 92 ter witness, I'm going to read, by way of introduction, the witness summary from our 65 ter filing sometime ago. Your Honour, the witness worked in the Bosnia-Herzegovina government's Directorate for Displaced Persons and Refugees in Sarajevo and in Zagreb during the period from roughly September of 1992 until the 31st of August, 1994. The ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia during this time period was Bisera Turkovic. The witness was responsible for refugee matters and dealt with the office for displaced persons and refugees of the Republic of Croatia - the Chamber may hear that referred to as ODPR - the director of which during this time was Mr. Rebic. The director -- also, she had dealings with the director of the collective centre for refugees at a place called Gasinci, Mr. Branko Vukoja. And also at the director of the collective centre for refugees on Obonjan Island, Mr. Miroslav Maslac. She also had dealings with various international organisations including the Red Cross; the Red Crescent; the office of Mr. Mazowiecki, the UN rapporteur; and various NGOs. Mr. Rebic was her principal contact in the Croatian government, relating to refugee matters. She also had dealings or knowledge of what she -- something that she knew of as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna for Refugees in Siroki Brijeg. The witness describes the Croatian authorities dealings with refugees, Muslim refugees in Croatia, including the treatment of Bosnian Muslim children vis-a-vis or in relationship or comparison to Bosnian Croats regarding schooling. She also touches upon the conditions and operations of refugee centres in Croatia and the transfer of various refugees from -- first of all, from Bosnia to Croatia and then in some instances, many instances, on to third countries. The witness learned of various of these topics from phone calls and contacts and interviews with various Bosnian Muslim refugees and their relatives. She required authorisation from Mr. Rebic's office to gain access to these centres and to see the refugees and have contact with them. She will talk in particular about two collective centres that being on the island of Obonjan and also at the Gasinci location. Gasinci was the largest, at least for a time, of the refugee centres with approximately 3.000 refugees, and again the director of that particular centre was Mr. Vukoja. The witness will also talk about the placement or transfer of Bosnian Muslim men who had been held for a time at various of the HVO detention camps, including the Heliodrom, Ljubuski, and Dretelj and how many of these men and some of their families were transferred to Croatia, and in some instances to third countries. She will also talk about the topic of the withdrawal of refugee status, the either withdrawal or termination of refugee status of Bosnian Muslims who had found themselves in Croatia from Bosnia-Herzegovina at various times, and the problems that presented to them and their continued living situation either in Croatia or going to a third country, or how it may have impacted their being returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina. She also had some limited dealings, Your Honour, with some humanitarian convoy issues. They will be touched upon in the course of her testimony. I think that's an overview of what the witness will address, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ms. Krajsek, with that in mind if I could ask you a few background questions, please, so that everyone in the courtroom will get to know you a bit better before I then show you your previous statements -- statement and ask you a couple -- some questions about that. Do I understand correctly that you graduated from the University of Sarajevo, from the faculty of economics in the area of marketing in 1977?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And from the time that you approximately -- some of these things just in terms of your background, some of the dates may not be exactly precise, but from the time of your graduation approximately 1977 until 1992, were you involved working for various public companies in the position of economist?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: That's correct. I worked in two public companies until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The second of those companies and your longest -- for the longest period of time at a company called Energoinvest?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, Ms. Krajsek, that in approximately August of 1992, you were approached by the person who was then the director of the Directorate for Displaced Persons and Refugees of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ms. Amila Omersoftic and asked you to begin working for that directorate?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you, in fact, began working for that directorate in approximately September 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that capacity, from approximately November of 1992 until the end of February 1993, you worked at the directorate in Sarajevo on a number of projects, and if I understood you correctly, you were very much involved in actually setting up the organisation and structure of the directorate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then is it correct that on approximately the 1st of March, 1993, until the 31st of August, 1994, you were transferred or received a new assignment to work in the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'll ask you a few more details about that in a few moments, but during that time did you become involved and have the principal responsibility in the embassy during that period for dealing with matters of refugees?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can have the assistance of the usher, please, to put the binder of materials in front of witness, and including her statement. I assume it's in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you in that binder to first of all turn to what's been marked as Exhibit 10124.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I do apologise. Your Honours, may I please have a two-minute break? I forgot my glasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we do not want to waste any court time, and whilst someone is getting your glasses, I have a question to put to you. You say you were working for the BiH embassy in Zagreb. Did you have the status of a diplomat when you were employed at the embassy in Zagreb? So you had the status of a diplomat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And another question generally as to the situation you were in. Do you know whether both Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia had ratified the Vienna Convention on consular relations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you want -- [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you wish to have this question clarified, I can have it clarified for you by way of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kovacic, it's very kind of you, but it was not a central point because the indictment does not claim violations of the Vienna Convention as a point the Defence is charged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I thought you were interested in terms of the status of the witness at the time in terms of the Vienna Convention, but whatever you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I appreciate your offer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, if I can ask you please, if you can now find 10124. I suspect it will be toward the back of your binder unless -- no, sorry, they placed it on top in this instance. Forgive me. 10124. And do you have that? She has it.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With that in front of you, madam, let me just ask you a few questions. Is it correct that you gave an interview to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY on the 27th, 28th, and 29th of November, 2004?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at that time you recall that a written statement was prepared in the English language and then interpreted to you or read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could ask you in Exhibit P 10124, the English version is on top, I believe, and if I could ask you to please turn your -- turn to page 19.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that your signature, please, immediately above the date 30 November 2004?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you leaf through the document, if you will, turn through some of the pages, is it also correct that you at that time initialed each page of the statement, and do you see your initials on this document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I placed my initials there, and I see them clearly on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, at the time you signed this statement on the 30th of November, 2004, madam, did you consider this statement to be a true and accurate statement to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And let me now switch to the Bosnian language version of your statement which you will also find, I believe, as part of Exhibit P 10124. Since arriving in The Hague did you have -- have you had an opportunity to review a version of your statement that has been put in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, with all that in mind, let me first of all go back, then, to the English -- in reference to the English version. I would like to confirm with the Chamber that you asked to make a number -- several, not very many, but a few corrections and if you could just confirm, please. In the paragraph, and I'm now referring specifically to the -- well, in this particular instance, it would apply to both versions but I'm particularly looking at the English version in any event. In paragraph 28, you indicated that in the list of cities or villages or locations that Vinkovci should be deleted; is that correct? Paragraph 28, Vinkovci or Vinkovci. Sorry, markings are not on that --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in reference to paragraph 50. Toward the end of that paragraph. It's a rather, perhaps small change, but you asked that it be -- the end of that sentence or the send of that paragraph should read: "Distributed questionnaires to Muslims imprisoned by HVO from the area of Mostar." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention, please, to paragraph number 67. If I understood correctly, you wish to delete the first sentence of paragraph 20 -- excuse me, 67, starting with the word "We," and ending with the word "Serbs." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally in terms of the English version, if you look at page -- or excuse me, paragraph 72 on the same page, in the first line of that sentence you again would -- you would request that the first sentence read: "Those who agreed to go to Turkey were offered to fill in a questionnaire." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I understand correctly, and more importantly can the Judges understand, that those are all the changes and corrections that you wish to make to the English version of your statement?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: You did understand things correctly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam, if we could then turn to the B/C/S version of your Bosnian language version, excuse me, of your statement. There are two attached -- essentially, the second document is the original Bosnian language version, and then behind -- after that set of 29 pages, in the middle of the overall document, then you come to a second version, if you will, of your Bosnian language statement starting again with page number 1, and did you also ask to make and were changes made in the Bosnian language version, which are indicated by either certain words in the hard-copy version of your statement being either omitted or deleted by being struck through, and new words are their replacements being indicated by being underlined? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: That is correct, and also the correction was done properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Simply to make it -- give one particular concrete example, in that version, which unfortunately I won't be able to read, but at least everyone in the courtroom can see an example of what's been done. If I can ask you in that version to turn to paragraph 72 on page 17. If you have that, madam, looking at paragraph 72, there are several -- there's a couple of words in the first line that have been struck and some additional words that have been inserted that are underlined, and does that reflect the changes that you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just -- if it may assist the Chamber, is it correct, madam, that there were some changes that you thought were particularly functions, if you will, or aspects of Bosnian language where you did not believe that the English language needed to be corrected but the particular usage of the Bosnian language, in your view, needed to be corrected, and that's why there may be changes in the Bosnian version that are not necessarily reflected in the English language document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, madam, having gone through your statements and having now noted the corrections in the record, let me ask you this: If -- concerning these -- this statement that you gave in 2004 as has now been corrected, if I were to ask you questions about all these matters or topics in court would the answers and the information that you gave in your statement 2004 as corrected, would that be your testimony in court?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: That would be my testimony in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. With that in mind, and, ma'am, you may need to speak up. You're speaking quite softly at times. It is being picked up on the record, but it may assist if you could speak a bit more loudly, please.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could just ask you some follow-up questions in reference to paragraph 12 of your statement where you talk about the time of your service during Zagreb. You say in your statement that you went to work there initially in connection with something called logistics centres. Can you just briefly tell us what the logistics centres were at that time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: At that time, the logistics centres were supposed to represent federal centres for the humanitarian aid arriving and which had to be distributed in an organised manner and transported throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And approximately how many of these logistics centres existed in the Republic of Croatia as of March of 1993 that were being operated on behalf -- by or on behalf of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: There were supposed to be four or five of those logistics centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Zagreb to take up your post, can you tell the Judges that -- did you find that after being there a short time that it did not -- it was not practical, you did not deem it practical to continue working in that area, that is, working in the topic or around the function of the logistics centres?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I learnt about that after 10 to 15 days of being in Zagreb, after I had collected basic information about the existence of the centres and whether their legal status was regulated in Croatia. And I also drew my opinion from the fact that I realised that the logistics centre in Ploce was not legalised in the port of Ploce. And according to my plan the organisation of logistical centres of the kind that I wanted to introduce and implement was supposed to be -- that was supposed to be one of the basic centres for the transport and distribution of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And based on what you found, did you believe that you could carry out your function, the original functions that had been tasked to you in terms of overseeing, if you will, these logistics centres?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: No. I realised that I couldn't do that, that I couldn't realise the goal that I wanted to when arriving, and I informed the government in Sarajevo about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you propose to return to Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I wasn't able to do the job that I was sent out to do and that I was willing to go back and work for the head office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And instead of being sent back to Sarajevo, was it at that time that your function essentially was -- your job description, as we might say now, was rewritten to task you into the area of dealing with refugees?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I would rather put it this way: That they appointed me attache for refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you say appointed you attache, were you an employee of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Precisely. That's when I became an employee of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during the time that you were working at the embassy and which is going to be the time we are going to be talking about in the course of your testimony, did you consider your superior or the person we might say boss to be the ambassador Ms. Turkovic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: That was my boss, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, one follow-up question, please. In this embassy in Zagreb, how many people were working with the ambassador, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really couldn't answer that, because all I knew was the number of people that worked in the part -- the department that I headed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In this embassy were there 10 people, 50, 200? Could you give us an order of magnitude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to guess, but it is my feeling that there might have been 20 people in the embassy, plus in the consul department, but I really don't know how many people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the benefit of the courtroom, I'm skipping over and not putting any additional questions to the witness concerning paragraphs 14 through 18 -- or 19, in the event that either the Court, or of course, the Defence can ask about any aspects of the statement, but just to make it clear, I'm not going into those topics further at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your statement, Ms. Krajsek, from approximately paragraph 20 to paragraph 27, you tell us about the -- your involvement in the embassy in connection with providing schooling, providing education, in particular for Muslim refugees in the Republic of Croatia. And you were involved in that issue or in carrying out and providing that service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, very intensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I just have one or two questions to clarify in that -- in those paragraphs. If I can direct your attention to paragraph number 24 of your statement. You mention in connection with these schools that were set up for the Bosniak or Muslim children something called the coordination of Islamic humanitarian organisations, that they financed the project, and then at the end of that paragraph, 24, you say: "Croatia never financed or co-financed these costs, which can be proved through documentation." Can I ask you just to confirm if you know, do I understand correctly then that in terms of providing the schooling for those Bosnian refugee children in Croatia, this was not financed or provided by the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: For all the children that were incorporated into exterritorial schools Croatia did not set aside any funds, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could ask you one clarifying question concerning paragraph 25. In paragraph 25 you said that -- of your statement you say that the "Croatian government brought a regulation according to which the children had to have a christening certification -- certificate in order to get in the regular school, a certificate that the Bosniaks obviously did not have." And my follow-up question to you about that is how long to your knowledge did that regulation continue in effect?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I don't know how long after my return to Bosnia-Herzegovina this stayed in force, but it was in force in the academic year of 1992 and 1993, and also from 1993 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm asking no additional questions about paragraphs 21 through 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a question on paragraph 25, please. On these christening certifications, Croatian children who would go to school in Zagreb, when they were admitted in the school, to your knowledge were they also asked to provide this christening certificate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to follow up on the president's question, in case some clarification might be helpful. As you indicate in your statement, I believe, but is it correct that in your experience you found that as to the Bosnian Croat refugees, those children were brought into or became part of the Croatian schools?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Can we ask non-leading questions at this point? I believe it's a follow-up to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Whatever Your Honours' desire is. It's a bit artificial, I submit, in this situation for me to simply ask her to read a paragraph of her additional statement or -- I can do that if that's what the Chamber would like me to do, but I think it's -- I'll go on because the statement, I think on these matters, speaks for itself. Unless the Chamber has additional questions on those paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, she was a representative of the embassy. I assume the embassy was for everyone who came from Bosnia-Herzegovina and not for just Muslims, and therefore I would suspect that part of her portfolio would have covered everyone, not just Muslims, so she should know those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 25 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in your job as attache at the embassy in charge of schooling issues, let me ask you the following: If a Bosnian Croat child who, for some reason, ended up in Zagreb, came to your embassy to get administrative information, or to obtain aid from his country's embassy, so was there a different treatment between different people, or did you deal with all the requests without taking into account the origin of the person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Quite literally we treated all requests equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To follow up, then, on that question, in connection specifically with schools and education, can you tell the Judges in your experience how did -- how was it that the Bosnian Croat refugee children were provided an education when they arrived in Zagreb or elsewhere in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they were included into the regular system of elementary education in the Republic of Croatia, with the exception of one coastal school which had children who were Bosnian Croats of origin but didn't want to be included into the exterritorial system of the schools of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but attended the school and curriculum according to the programme applied in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, there may be a misunderstanding or translation or transcription error. I believe my question was in terms of specifically the Bosnian Croat children and whether they were provided an education in the -- how they were provided, and you said to the best of your knowledge in the regular system of elementary education in the Republic of Croatia, and then you pointed out an exception, what you described, I believe, as a coastal school, but it wasn't clear how that was an exception. You seem to go ahead then and make a description, if I read this correctly, that those children in fact did go also into the regular schools of the Republic of Croatia. So I think there may be a mistake or a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I'll try and make myself clearer. To the best of my knowledge, the children of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were Croats went to regular Croatian primary schools and elementary schools. The only group of Bosnian Croats, that is to say, children who were not included into the regular schools of Croatia as far as I know were children from the area of Bugojno. They had fled from Bugojno and were displaced persons and located somewhere along the coast in Makarska, around Makarska. They were organised in what we call exterritorial schools, which were not within the framework and network of the BH schools, BH exterritorial schools in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I'm going to now direct your attention forward -- I'm skipping over a number of paragraphs, and in connection with paragraph 33, in paragraph 33 you begin talking about the Obonjan refugee centre. This refugee centre was on Obonjan Island on the Croatian coast; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you have any understanding of approximately how long -- for how long, if it was, prior to your arrival in Zagreb in March 1993 that Obonjan had been operated as a refugee centre?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I really don't have official data. The centre was opened in March 1993 when I arrived, and talking to the refugees that I encountered there I gained the impression that they had been there for three or four months already before my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where were these refugees from, the ones that were there when you first visited the centre.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: From the interior of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say interior of Bosnia, might that also be referred to as Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the refugees that you encountered there, were these Croats or Muslims or both?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Exclusively Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, madam, in paragraph 35 of your statement you mention that at Obonjan, the facility was guarded or secured by what you describe as special police of the Croatian Ministry of Interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges generally about the refugee centres that you were most familiar with at the time, both at Obonjan and also at Gasinci, whether the refugees of these collection centres, were they free to move about, did they have freedom of movement or were they restricted to these camps?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: In that respect the centre on the island of Obonjan was quite specific. On that island all the refugees were able to move around freely, around the island freely, but weren't able to cross to the mainland for a number of reasons. The first limiting factor was they had to pay for the boat between Sibenik and the island, and they didn't have the money to do so, for the ferry. And I think that they had to ask permission from the director of the collective centre as well, if they wanted to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how about at the Gasinci centre?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: In Gasinci, the freedom of movement was different. The regime was different, because it was a centre that was on the mainland and not far from the town of Djakovo. So they could go out into town and come back if they were back by the time prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraphs 42 to 44, you talk about certain development projects at Obonjan. Just to clarify that point, can you explain if you know whether the Croatian government, to your knowledge, was financing or financially supporting the refugee centre for Muslims on Obonjan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask what the relevance is of all these questions? I mean, the freedom of movement, for instance. Perhaps she can tell us under international law or whatever law she understands, do refugees usually go walkabout in a country where they're hosted as refugees? And in this instance, what is whether Croatia under those circumstances was providing infrastructure in this particular place or any other place? What exactly was her portfolio, and what exactly does this have to do with the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, several things, Your Honour, in response. Number one, I admit to in part being -- anticipating a bit of cross-examination based on various questions that have been raised in the past year, and certain statements and positions taken by certain of the accused on the extensive benefits provided by the Croatian government to Bosnian Muslim refugees. But we can possibly wait till redirect to deal with that if those questions are, in fact, put. However, however, the condition of the camps, the support of the camps, what was happening in Croatia is directly relevant to the fact, in the Prosecution's view, that there was tremendous pressure put then to move these refugees or cause them to be moved on to third countries and not for them to be returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is why, among other things, we believe it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, if they're going to go in that route, I wish to remind the Court that perhaps the Prosecution will need then to describe exactly the conditions, because we're talking about being -- having them in hotels, having them in houses, and there were instances where they were being encouraged to go into tents. And what -- how in that -- how is that relevant? And of course, if that is the case, I suspect with this -- with this particular witness they might be able to tell us how many -- how many refugees was Croatia capable of absorbing, how many it had at the time, and perhaps how many it was trying to get rid of, because I think these are important issues that must be addressed if they're going to go down that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's save time. To your knowledge, Witness, how many refugees were there coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina? Just give us an order of magnitude, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the estimates in 1993 spoke of the fact that there were 300.000 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of these 300 -- 300.000 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, there must have been refugees from different backgrounds, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. Could you give us the breakdown in percentage according to their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I am afraid I'm not able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question then: You spoke about two centres, one on the island Obonjan, and Gasinci. One is on an island, and the other one is on land, on the mainland. So there was quite an interesting question asked by Mr. Scott, but he didn't go into detail. I'd like to know whether these refugees had total freedom of movement. I mean when you're a refugee you can to move around, you're allowed to move around. So to your knowledge, did they have complete freedom of movement or did they need some kind of permit from MUP, from the MUP or from camp authorities to move around. Or were they allowed to take the train or to move around freely throughout Croatia, to go to the beach if need be, if they wanted to go. To your knowledge was there complete freedom of movement or did those 300.000 refugees have to stay in very restricted geographical areas that were controlled?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the refugee centres had their house rules and the refugees were duty-bound to abide by them and they had refugee cards or IDs and with those they were allowed to move around Croatia freely, at least at certain periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in other words, a Muslim refugee was allowed to move around as to this refugee card or ID. This Muslim refugee, was he allowed to move around freely throughout the Republic of Croatia? For example, meet with you in the embassy if they needed to meet with you? Were they allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now a quarter to 4.00. It's time for a tea break, and we will resume at five after 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, I'm moving on to July of 1993, and by way of reference for both yourself and the courtroom, I direct your attention to paragraph 52 of your statement. You indicate in paragraph 52 of your statement that in total a bit less than a thousand Muslims from Mostar came to Croatia between the 18th and the 21st of July, 1993. This group was split and directed to Gasinci and the island of Obonjan. And my first question to you about this particular topic is how did you first come to know that these people, these Muslims from Mostar, had arrived in Croatia at these two camps?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: These expelled Muslims who arrived got permission from the authorities for refugees to make telephone calls to the embassy and then I learned from these telephone calls that a group arrived in Gasinci first. They were the first to call me, and then I got a telephone call from the island of Obonjan and so that is how I received information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 -- excuse me, my apology. In paragraph 49, you indicate that on the 21st of July you actually went to Gasinci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did you -- excuse me. How did you make the arrangements to do that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I had the general consent of Mr. Adalbert Rebic who was the representative of the office for refugees and expellees of the Republic of Croatia that I could enter the collection centres where the refugees were put up. On the basis of that authority issued by him I went to the centre in Gasinci, and as always, I first reported to -- well, the management, the director of these collective centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as indicated again in paragraph 49 of your statement, was the director of the Gasinci centre Mr. Branko Vukoja? If I pronounce it wrong, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct. That was the director.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you in this regard in the binder -- excuse me, bundle, binder of documents that you have in front of you, could you please go to Exhibit 3617. And as I've explained to you before, madam, in all instances I believe you'll find the English translation on top, and then you'll find the Bosnian language version beneath it. Do you have Exhibit 3617?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I have that document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- tell the Judges, please, what that document is?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: This is a document, information that I had drafted concerning an official trip, and on the basis of this I made a report that had to do with what happened on the dates of my official trip, and the report was made for the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia and also for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The report was used for other purposes as well, for further communication with international organisations whose representatives were present at the meeting that was held in Gasinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your statement, in paragraphs 50 to 56 of your statement, you set out a description of what had happened to these persons and how they had come to be transferred from Mostar to Croatia on this occasion. Both in your report, which is Exhibit 3617 and item number 2, some parts of your report are numbered, and if you look at item number 2, and also in paragraph 51 of your statement, you indicate that these people, the people coming from Mostar, were told that arrangements had been made for them to transfer -- to be transferred on to third countries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did you find -- well, if you know, what did they find? What did they report to you, and what did you find in connection with whether, in fact, arrangements were in place to immediately transport these people on to third countries from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Well, at the meeting that I wrote this information about, from document 3617, I had received information from expelled citizens that before they left Bosnia-Herzegovina they had received information that their displacement was being carried out in cooperation with the BH embassy in Croatia that had already taken certain measures to organise their further displacement in third countries. That was the first time I received such information, and of course, I informed them that the embassy is totally unprepared and that we had not gone into any kind of organisation of this kind because we had not expected them to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just ask a question for clarification. You speak of a meeting, this meeting. Could you give us some information on who attended the meeting and where it was held? I may have overlooked something, but I did not find that information in your statement. I'm referring to paragraph 12 of your statement, for instance, but it comes again at other instances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I'm trying to find the original of the report. In the second paragraph of document 3617, or, rather, my report, it says that the representatives of the embassy on the 21st of July had a meeting at the Gasinci refugee centre that was attended by representatives of the UNHCR, the International Red Cross Committee, the federation of the International Red Cross and Crescent of the Red Cross of Croatia as well and that the meeting was also attended by the representatives of Gasinci, Mr. Branko Vukoja. That is a meeting that was attended by all these representatives and -- well, not all of them, but it was also attended by as many expelled citizens as could fit into the room where the meeting was being had held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, I hope I won't offend you if I ask you to perhaps slow down just a bit. I think you're speaking quite quickly. You seem to have gone from a bit slow to now quite fast. So if we can find kind of a happy middle ground that would be, I think, helpful to everyone, including the interpreters. Let me go back to the question I asked you before Judge Trechsel's question. Perhaps I didn't state it clearly. When you looked into these matters or based on further conversations that you had with the persons who arrived from Mostar around this time, can you tell the Judges did you find that in fact the papers -- the paperwork was in place for these persons to be transferred at that time to third countries?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I received information through direct contact with the expellees that they were supposed to fill out certain forms that had been offered to them by the HVO, that they were also supposed to sign a document that -- well, that they leave all their properties to Herceg-Bosna and that this was a prerequisite for setting them free from different prisons where they had been detained. And the next prerequisite was that they had to leave their places of residence, that they had to go through Croatia to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you next to go to Exhibit 3655.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene again, Mr. Scott, but I think your question has not really been answered. You asked about documents being prepared for transfer to third countries, whereas the witness has informed us on documents that were prepared when the refugees were leaving Herceg-Bosna, and perhaps I repeat your question. To go to a third country there must be certain documents like entry visas or invitations or agreements that a third country is prepared to accept a certain amount of refugees. Were you aware whether any such documents existed? Was everything ready for continuation of the -- of the journey of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment nothing was prepared for the continuation of their journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, you're absolutely correct, and I appreciate the assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, with that in mind, madam, if you could then go to Exhibit 3655. And can you just -- I'm going to show you various documents, hopefully some of them fairly quickly, madam, and if you can just it tell us what that document is.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: This is a letter from the embassy, the office for refugees, that we sent to the UNHCR, the Zagreb office, and through this letter we informed the UNHCR that we had asked the director of the head office for displaced persons and refugees of the government of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Adalbert Rebic, to arrange a meeting in order to openly discuss and find a solution for exiled Mostar citizens temporarily accommodated in the refugee centre of Gasinci, and through direct contacts with this office we were trying to reach a solution to the problems that we faced once they had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could next ask you to go to 3656. The next -- it should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before moving on to the next document, I have a question about document 3655, Witness, the document you have in front of you, the document signed by the ambassador. What I find interesting here is who wrote this document, and I'm wondering whether you were not the author of this document, because here we see AMB/ZAG-AK. So I'm thinking AK might be your initials. Were you the person who drafted this document, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I am the person who drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what we see here, ZAG, what does it stand for, ZAG?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means this was the BH embassy in Zagreb. Zagreb was an abbreviation for the actual locality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So you are the person who drafted the document, and then the document was signed by the ambassador. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we could go on, madam, to 3656, and your previous -- the letter that you drafted was dated the 23rd of July, and if you look at 3656, was a similar letter or at least another letter sent that day over the signature of the ambassador to Mr. Rebic about the arrival of these people from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have 3656?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just let me come at it this way then, following on the President's question: Is this a letter that you also prepared for the ambassador's signature addressed to Mr. Rebic of the Croatian Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask you to go to Exhibit 3708.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott. May I ask an intermediary question? Witness, is there any relation between these two documents 3656 and 3655?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is the very same subject matter, although the UNHCR office in Zagreb was in receipt of a copy of 3656. Nevertheless, a separate letter was prepared for the UNHCR, too, providing information concerning the subject matter that was of interest to us and why we were asking Mr. Rebic for a meeting at his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm looking at these two letters, and I see that there is a slight shift from one to the other. In the first letter, 3655, that's in English, of course I don't know what word you used in your own language, but in English we see that there is a mention of "exiled citizens of Mostar," and in the report that you also drafted, document 3617, you also use the word of "exiled" in English. But now when we look at the letter sent to Mr. Rebic, we that these "exiled" have turned into "expelled" in English, expelled persons. Is this deliberate from your part, or is it the case where the English translation is not quite true to the original, because the term "exiled" means something different than "expelled." You can be exiled on a voluntary basis, but when you've been expelled from somewhere there's nothing voluntary about it. Was there a shift here in the way these words were used by yourself or is it a matter of translation, of interpretation, where a mix-up has happened, a confusion between the words "exiled" and "expelled"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We very specifically referred to displaced citizens from Mostar, expelled, as 3656 says. I believe that this is a language mistake in the letter that was sent to the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you spell in your language, in B/C/S, the word for expelled? What is the word for expelled in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Protjeran, a person who did not leave his residence of his own free will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a slight concern here. You were working for the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb, in Croatia, and you were in charge of receiving or welcoming the citizens of your country in Croatia, and I see in your letter that they were escorted by the police of the Republic of Croatia. That's what we read in the letter dated 23rd of July, 1993. And I have the following question about this: I'd like to know whether you had a look at the documents that your citizens had in their possession to enter on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, because you yourself were not a citizen of that republic. What sort of documents did they have to allow them to enter the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina that we are talking about did not have any individual documents on them. Looking for documents on the basis of which they entered the Republic of Croatia in the first place, I turned to the director of Gasinci asking on the basis of what he allowed such a big group of people to enter the centre, and on the basis of which documents he had put them up at the centre. He then showed me a list of these citizens who had entered. When I asked to be given a copy of the list and the accompanying documents, he never responded. He promised verbally, but the embassy and I never got an appropriate document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, we do not know who gave these citizens from Bosnia and Herzegovina the authorisation to enter Croatia. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are not quite right, because we got the following document: The transit visa that was issued by the office for expellees and refugees of the government of Croatia, headed by Mr. Adalbert Rebic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
