utterances.text: Going back or continuing on with Exhibit 3708, if we can, can you tell us whether that is the response that your embassy received from Mr. Rebic to the earlier letter?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, that is the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to go to the end of the third paragraph, and I don't know -- let me just check. It's also the end of -- yes. Different page number, but it's the third paragraph of the letter. At the end of that Mr. Rebic says that -- makes the allegation that no one had gone to deal with the Bosnian Croats expelled -- or refugees from the Lasva Valley. And can you tell the Chamber whether that was a true statement or not?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge this is quite incorrect. The ambassador, with a few other officers from our embassy, went to Split immediate, to Poljub [phoen], having learned that there were citizens from the Lasva Valley that had arrived there. They were a priority visit for me, and I visited them as soon as I could in Pineta [phoen], at the collection centre where they had been put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask you to go to Exhibit 3765, and can you just confirm to us that was a response from the Ambassador Turkovic to Mr. Rebic's letter?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just intervene right now for a second. Again, I don't see -- I fail to see the relevance of all of this. Is the Croatia -- Croatian government, and by that I mean the State of Croatia, are they now being charged with failure to provide adequate assistance to the refugees? That's number one. Number two, is Mr. Rebic a member of the joint criminal enterprise by virtue of his occupation? I really fail to see -- apparently the two individuals, including this -- this witness, may have had their run-ins and disagreements, however, I don't see how that is relevant to the indictment. Perhaps we could have some guidance. So I'm objecting on grounds of relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, is Mr. Rebic a member of the joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the indictment, I'm just having a chance to try to look at it, but clearly it is part of the Prosecution case that, since counsel asked me directly and I'll respond directly, yes, that this was part of the ethnic cleansing of Muslims from Bosnia and Herzegovina and from the Herceg-Bosna area. This was part of a system, as charged in the indictment, to move Muslims out of Herceg-Bosna, and it was done any number of ways. One of those ways was to move them either -- at least temporarily into Croatia and either to abandon them there, which may come up further in parts of the testimony of this witness, or to move them on to other countries, but not to return them to Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, yes, it is absolutely part of the indictment and part of the charges in this case that this was one form of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that answer, as I understand the indictment, the Prosecution has indicted, along with the six accused here, the late President Tudjman, the late Mr. Susak, the late Bobetko, and the late Mate Boban, and we could say that they are unindicted co-conspirators if you want to put it that way, or they have been indicted, they're just not alive to be here. Be that as it may, it would seem to me now, based on this answer, that the Prosecution has to show some linkage between President Tudjman or any of the other members of the joint criminal enterprise and Mr. Rebicic at this point -- Rebic, at this point. And I must say that in light of that answer, it would appear that the State of Croatia, not just individuals, but now we're talking about the State of Croatia was engaged in a joint criminal enterprise. So that's why I don't use the word "government" so we're not confused with personalities. But now we're talking about a state. And I find that this is getting far afield. I again object on the grounds of relevancy, just as I objected earlier on the grounds of relevancy with respect to education.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, for one thing -- and I don't think we should get into these lengthy discussions with the witness here and spend the witness's time talking about this. If the Chamber would like to schedule a time to talk about the JCE and the theories of JCE and the charges of the indictment, we can do that. But I don't think we should have a witness on the stand, for a lengthy discussion of that. I've answered the Chamber's question. I think the indictment is quite clear: Deportation is charged. Deportation involves moving across international boundaries. Paragraph -- I'm just looking very quickly. Paragraph 225 talks about a system of ill-treatment for deporting Muslims to other countries. Yes, indeed, Your Honour it's part of the indictment and it's part of the forms of ethnic cleansing that are charged in the indictment. You can ethnically cleanse people by burning them out of their homes and killing them; you can also ethnically cleanse them by sending them somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want to debate the point but I would assume that the Prosecution bears the burden of proof and one burden of proof is that Croatia could absorb more refugees and was systematically engaged in some sort of deportation once refugees came there. So that's why I'm saying unless we have more evidence from the -- from the Prosecution how they intend to link all of this, I think at this point this sort of testimony, these sorts of letters between two personalities is not relevant. But I welcome the opportunity at some other point to have a debate or have a discussion on JCE. I think that would be most appropriate, because we need to narrow the scope of where this trial is going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can resume, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, madam, you were asked a few moments ago because we finished with 3765, and I just wanted to -- the Chamber to have that full exchange of correspondence and how it will relate to -- indeed, link up to other issues in the case. You mentioned in paragraph 54 of your statement, and you may refer to this in one of your -- excuse me, one of your answers to questions from the Judges. You say in paragraph 54, the Mostar group convoy was accompanied by a fax from Professor Rebic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you please to look at Exhibit 10048. And can you tell us what that document is, please?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: This is a document which was compiled by the governmental department for refugees of the Republic of Croatia. It is approval for entry and temporary stay in the Republic of Croatia for a group of expelled persons -- or, rather, the office allows entry for persons from Mostar for temporary sojourn, and it mentions 500 persons who will be temporarily accommodated at Gasinci centre near Djakovo. So that's like a transit visa for a temporary stay or, rather, in order to cross over the territory of Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please to look at the last sentence of Mr. Rebic's document dated the 16th of July, 1993, issued in Zagreb, and it says: "...therefore, have no right to obtain refugee status in Republic of Croatia." As the attache at the Bosnia embassy in Zagreb dealing with refugee issues, can you tell us what was the significance or consequence to these people of not obtaining refugee status in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: At the time we were thinking along two lines. We didn't know what their status would be, on the one hand, and that's why we approached international organisations for their assistance. And on the other hand, we already had information according to which the Croatian police was arresting BH refugees, even those who had proper ID cards and documents which showed that they were registered as refugees. So we were highly concerned for their safety during that temporary sojourn in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And going back to the question that Judge Trechsel clarified and put to you better than I did earlier, did you find when these people arrived in mid -- in the second half of July, 1993, had the paperwork been put in place for them to move on immediately out of Croatia to a third country, or were they stuck in Croatia without refugee status?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Well, quite literally they were stuck. I never had a document preparing for their move to third countries. It never arrived. Such documents didn't reach me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to go to Exhibit 10052.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I have a question, Witness, to follow up, and I'd rather ask it now. Otherwise, we might lose track of what we are talking about. You were talking about refugees, and you just said that Mr. Rebic's letter states that these persons would not benefit from the status of refugees. I'm not sure you know the law on refugees governing -- for the Republic of Croatia, but there's the convention of July 28, 1951 on refugees, and this convention had been ratified by a great number of countries, including the former Yugoslavia, and a refugee can ask to get the status of refugee when he comes from another state when he believes that he may be persecuted for a number of criteria that are stated in this convention. So to your knowledge, the Republic of Croatia towards BiH refugees, did it refuse them, to acknowledge them as refugees? This is what this document seems to state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. And not the ones that were in this group of 500, but I know about many individual cases, too, in which refugees were not able to have refugee status and therefore were under the protection of the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yourself as member of the BiH embassy, did you get grievances from citizens of BiH who wanted to benefit from the status of refugee to stay and to remain in Croatia and couldn't because the government of Croatia did not want to grant them that status? Did you have any specific cases you could tell us about of people that actually complained about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had very many contacts. I had telephones calls, and people would come to the office for refugees, people who didn't manage to acquire refugee status or, rather, who were refused refugee status, and in situations like that we always sent those people to the UNHCR. We told them to contact them, and the UN Human Rights Unit, Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki. I can't remember all the names of the different institutions, but unfortunately that's as far as we could go. We couldn't do anything else for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, if I could ask you next to go to Exhibit P 10052. And -- sorry. The President just asked you whether you received any communications or grievances from some of these people about their situation, and can you tell the Judges what this document is, in fact, 10052?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: This is a document which on behalf of the 500 expelled citizens of Mostar was written to the BH embassy in Zagreb, and these expelled citizens of Mostar describe the situation they find themselves in on the island and provide information about the events that took place before they were expelled from Mostar. They explain that many of them were held at Heliodrom, what the HVO authorities offered them and Herceg-Bosna authorities offered them, and what offers they were made to leave detention. And they said that the HVO and the HZ HB offered them transit visas through the Republic of Croatia on condition that it was their intention to move on to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In particular, if I can ask you to go to I think what would be paragraph number five in the letter. It's the paragraph that begins with the words, at least -- I'm not sure about the exact translation, but, "Although everyone was skeptical." Can you tell me when -- if you can find that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the second sentence of that paragraph, referring to what you just said a moment ago, it says: "Only after they had boarded the buses were they told that they were going to Sibenik. Heavy police forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna escorted the convoy as far as Sibenik but was taken over by the police of the Republic of Croatia. All of these families were taken to the island of Obonjan." Skipping a few sentences. "None of them were prepared for this kind of abode since they had been promised transit through the Republic of Croatia en route to third countries. However, it is obvious that nothing will come of it." Now, this letter that you received from this group of individuals, you or the ambassador, the items that are reported in the letter, including the one that I just read to you, was that consistent with the information that you were receiving around this same time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Completely. Yes, it corresponds completely to the information that we were receiving and also from our telephone conversations with the expelled persons who were at Obonjan at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to go to 5064. First of all, madam, can you tell the Judges whether from your involvement with these issues and talking with the people that were arriving from Mostar, did you ever hear the name Biljana Nikic, or see it in documents?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I did see that name in some of the documents that we came across.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This statement, Ms. Nikic says: "On the 20th of July, 1993, I organised the departure of 150 people to the Republic of Croatia in order for them to take refuge in Obonjan near Sibenik." And is that consistent with what you saw happening on the ground when these people from Mostar arrived between the 18th and the 21st of July at Obonjan?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but could you repeat your question and tell me what you mean when you say whether that's what I saw. You mean the documents or the people?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. The report Ms. Nikic is making here, is that consistent with the information you received about the arrival of these people at Obonjan around this time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on to paragraph 58 -- or moving to paragraph 58 of your statement. You say: "With the Mostar group coming to Gasinci, the situation became even worse. The Mostar group and the refugees there started to be physically mistreatment -- mistreated. Quite often we were informed by the refugees that they had been beaten by locals, police officers, and even soldiers." Now, you mention that you were receiving information from the refugees, but can you say a bit more? Can you tell the Judges how it was that you and the embassy were receiving this information?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: A permanent organised contact was established with our refugees, and it was implemented in the following way: Within the total number of extraterritorial schools organised for refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in both of these collective centres, we also had a school, and we maintained permanent contact with the teaching staff as we did with the mothers. Usually it was the mothers that were present, the mothers of children going to those schools. So that was a constant source of information for us. Apart from this source of information, the refugees on an individual basis would decide to contact the embassy either in writing or orally. And of course, I would go into the field, I would make tours and visit the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to document 4150. And if you have that, can you tell the Judges what that document is?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: This is a report which relates to the problems of citizens of -- in the Republic of Croatia, and it was prepared for the Foreign Ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a copy was also sent to the head office for displaced persons and refugees, or the directorate, and it provides detailed information about the problems not only of the refugee population but also of the BH citizens who did not have their status in Croatia regulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to the third paragraph of your letter or report, and it says: "Every success of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is accompanied with a reaction of the authorities - police of the Republic of Croatia towards our citizens (searches, imprisonment, incarceration, arrests, sentences to expulsions, deportation - and forced returns to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina)." What information did you have about that, in connection with that part of your report?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I received information from the field, from the BH citizens themselves who were in some kind of jeopardy, either because they didn't have their status regulated in the Republic of Croatia or for other reasons, because they were present and witnessed arrests, the formation of groups for which it was said when they were formed that they would be deported. And then they contacted the embassy because they were afraid that they would suffer the same fate. So that was mostly how I come by the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to look to the -- I believe the fifth paragraph of the document. It begins with the words: "With the aim of protecting citizens." If you have that, madam. The last sentence in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The last sentence in that paragraph appears to indicate that 450 refugees had gone missing. Can you tell the Judges whether the -- what had happened to those 450 people or their whereabouts? Did you ever learn that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I didn't receive any feedback, information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving to paragraph 84 of your statement. You indicate there that on about the 27th and the 30th of August, 1993, a group of Muslims arrived from Ljubuski, approximately 551 persons. Can you tell the Judges what you learned about that and, again, how that came to your information -- or knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: The people from these groups who arrived were left in front of the mosque in Zagreb, and individuals from those groups would always ring up the embassy and tell us how many of them there were, where they were, and of course asked that somebody come to help them from the embassy, to help them find their way, see what they were going to do next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You mention a number of additional facts in your statement which I won't go into, particularly in paragraph 86. Many of these have been imprisoned -- men have been imprisoned in Heliodrom. If I can ask you to look at paragraphs 87 and 88. Can you tell the Judges what you found out, or what they found out in terms of whether, again, upon their arrival in Zagreb they had their -- the necessary paperwork existed for their immediate transportation on to a third country?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: They came to Croatia thinking that they had all the necessary visas for Germany, but since they weren't able to travel on with those visas, they contacted the embassy and informed us of the problem they were facing, and then we would ring up the German embassy, and the German embassy told us that they didn't have the proper visas for Germany. And the German embassy also told us that they already had information that these visas had been forged, visas that Bosnian-Herzegovinian citizens used to leave the country. And in my statement I set out the information I received when talking to our citizens, that these were visas which always arrived through the same fax machines with two lawyers and a photographer from Ljubuski. And the visas and letters of guarantee were always issued by the same person, and the German embassy told me that they were not able to identify any such person in Germany, that they didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to how these faxed documents were then actually distributed to various Bosnian Muslim people in the Ljubuski area? How did they get from the lawyer's office, if you will, into the hands of the Muslims themselves?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: According to what the BH citizens that I was in contact with told me, these documents were distributed by military policemen, and members of their families could also collect these documents in the building of the municipality of Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to document -- or Exhibit P 04620. In other words, 4620. And can you tell us -- when you have that document, please, can you tell us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I have the document in front of me. This is information sent from the department for refugees to the directorate of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for displaced persons and refugees about what we knew, namely that a new group of expelled citizens from Ljubusko had arrived. They arrived on the 29th of August, 1993. They arrived in Zagreb then. And it was a group of 133 expelled citizens. I have provided information here that they left according to the same pattern, if I put it -- if I can put it that way. They were received on Nedjo Galic's fax. He was the photographer. And also to the fax machines of two lawyers. Grgic Misko and Dubravko, and these were actually documents that the expelled citizens from Ljubuski had established were invalid and they realised that they could not travel to third countries with these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to next look at document 4603. And as soon as you have that, madam, can you tell us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I have the document in front of me, and it is information about expelled citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the municipality of Ljubuski that were sent to UN organisations, namely the UNHCR, the centre for human rights, the International Red Cross and the International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent. We provided accurate information here, of course on the basis of what we knew at all, namely that we knew that 551 persons were expelled from the territory of the municipality of Ljubuski. We also provided information about the locations where these expellees were put up. At that point we knew that they were put up at the Nermina restaurant, at the Park Hotel in Dugo Selo, and we knew that quite a few of them were put up in refugee centres in the territory of the city of Zagreb, generally speaking. In addition to providing information through this document, we asked each and every one of these individual organisations to do their best in order to help put up these citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, ma'am, can you indicate of what -- of what nation or ethnic group were these 551 persons who arrived from Ljubuski around this time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: We are talking about 551 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you go to the fourth paragraph of your report, please, your letter, it's the one that begins with the words "Transit visas." And at the end of that paragraph it's going on about the transit visas and it says: "They were issued --" excuse me, "on which it is written they can stay in the Republic of Croatia 48 hours." And then the next paragraphs: "According to the statements of individuals, they have been told that for them there are guarantee letters and that they are going to Germany. Later, upon entry in the Republic of Croatia, all of those have learnt that those guarantee letters are valid only for leaving Ljubuski and coming to Zagreb." Can you tell the Judges if you know what happened to these 551 persons after their -- after their 48 hours were up?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I probably only have part of this information available. I know that some asked for help from us and the UNHCR to be sent to third countries, and that is how they left Croatia. Part of these people continued to have problems because they were moving about Croatia without appropriate documents. They were arrested, and I don't know about their fate after that. At any rate, they left Croatia organised to a lesser extent by the UNHCR. To my mind it was NGOs really that became more active and that helped them leave Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please to go to document 5053. Again, this is a document from Biljana Nikic. She was a trained economist, was she? Had the same background as yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the text of the document that begins: "On the 10th of September 1993 while conducting my regular job," when she says she was engaged at the Croatian Community or Republic of Herceg-Bosna office for expelled persons and refugees in Mostar. "While conducting my regular job, I received a female client who showed me the permit to leave the city. The permit was issued and signed by Pavlovic, Bozo, authorising her to travel from Mostar to Germany via the Republic of Croatia. Change of residency was given as the reason for travel. "In my opinion this should not be done because it leaves written evidence, which is nothing else but a legalisation of ethnic cleansing. If the International Humanitarian Organisation would find about this it would cause a great deal of problems." And as someone involved with these issues and having received these people in Croatia, would you agree with the assessment made by Ms. Nikic that this was a form of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Your Honour, I object to the form of the question. Obviously she's being asked to speculate and we don't know who this Pavlovic was, what his role was, whether he was doing it for that purpose. I suggest the question is improper as formed and she's not competent to testify to these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think she can -- in her field as the attache at the embassy, a woman who is working in the area of refugees and based on what she has seen happen and what you've already heard this afternoon with these people coming from Mostar, from Ljubuski, and elsewhere, that she is able to give an assessment what was happening here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: She's being asked, first of all, to give a legal opinion. Second of all, she's being asked to going into somebody's mind and thoughts and to decipher what exactly this person meant. I think the document speaks for itself. She certainly is not competent. She hasn't met this woman. She haven't discussed the issues, and I can go on. And I feel that this question is not relevant for this particular witness. Now, they can bring in Ms. Nikic or somebody else and perhaps that may be the appropriate witness to answer that question, but not this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you might have asked the witness whether she knew Bozo Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can do that, Your Honour. I was also going to ask her because I think she answered this earlier, but let me in the current context ask her again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This person, Biljana Nikic, did you know that name and her involvement in these issues from either reports that you had seen or information you received from the refugees?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: On the basis of documents that I received from refugees, I knew of Mrs. Nikic because her name appeared in documents, and I saw her name typed out, and I even saw her signatures on some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to follow up on the President's question, did you have any knowledge of this man Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any information that this was the fictitious person in Germany whose name apparently was on all the forged or false transit documents?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I cannot recall the name exactly of this fictitious person. I don't think that the person that I knew as having issued documents en masse was Bozo Pavlovic. I know another name, but I cannot remember any other names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, if you do happen to remember that name, perhaps you can assist us while you're still here in The Hague. Moving forward, in paragraph 107 of your statement, you mention that around the 14th of September, 1993, there was an agreement, a cease-fire agreed by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Tudjman, if you see that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Precisely. I have it right in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask you to go to Exhibit 5051.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the speaker. We're sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, madam, the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I have found the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that a copy of the agreement or at least one of the versions setting out the agreement between Mr. -- President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic on the 14th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your statement, paragraph 107, you mention that pursuant to this agreement various working groups were formed, and if you will look at, starting around paragraph numbered 4 of the agreement itself and following, do you see that the agreement indeed provides for the organisation of a number of working groups?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you identify any of the particular working groups that are listed here of which you became a member?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: It is the working group from paragraph I -- paragraph II, subparagraph 1, and it had to do with humanitarian status related and other issues pertaining to the position of refugees and displaced persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia and also regarding their return to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, we could also refer to that -- is it correct that would be Article II, paragraph number 1?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And apart from yourself on the Bosnian -- or on behalf of the government of the Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Angovic, the lawyer at the embassy in your department, is he also part of this working group?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Mr. Angovic who was a lawyer was also a member of this working group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in paragraph 107 of your statement you indicate that the persons appointed or named on the Bosnian Croat side, is it correct, was Mr. Kresimir Zubak and Mr. Darinko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this context, madam, I would like you to look next at Exhibit 5080.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And madam, this is a record of the meeting in the offices of President Tudjman on the 15th of September, 1993, the day after he had signed the agreement with President Izetbegovic. And if I can ask you to go down where the text starts under the word "President." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It says, "I welcome the delegation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Gentlemen, I invited you here to inform you as to what preceded the Geneva agreement. "Croatia was under pressure, official pressure, from the European Union as a whole and from individual states. Over the past 14 days, I received at least five or six official notes from the European Union, United States of America, France, and Germany. They all requested that we make as many concessions to the Muslims as possible, and they all threatened us with sanctions because of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "They even went as far as sending us a warning that they would cancel our special guest status at the European Council Assembly. "In such /as printed/, they clearly put your camps and humanitarian convoys and so on in the first place." In your role, involvement in humanitarian issues and specifically refugee issues at the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb during this time, were you aware of the pressure, the international pressure that was being brought to bear on the Republic of Croatia because of what was happening in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object here. I object to the form of the question and the way in which it was stated. First, the Prosecution, in a very leading fashion, reads a presidential transcript, thereby tainting the witness, and then asks her whether what he read comports with her memory. It should be the other way around. Now, the presidential transcript can come in. It can come in through other witnesses. In fact, they have someone who was working for the Office of the Prosecutor who is going to analyse these documents. But I do find it objectionable to first to read a document that contains information and then ask the witness to verify it. It's similar to calling for a yes or no answer. It's leading and I object to this. I waited, I didn't want to interrupt him. But I object, and I think that given that he has led the witness, at this point in time he needs to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, document 5080 might already have been admitted through another witness. I'm not quite sure, because we've had so many transcripts or notes related to Mr. Tudjman's meeting. I'm not quite sure any more. But as Mr. Karnavas was saying, the witness here is not familiar with the document, but she might be aware of a very specific fact or event that is mentioned in this document. Then this document might prove useful. But in that case, you have to ask a question that is not a leading question, a question about that particular event. You have to say, for example, "This document is related to this event. Does that -- is that in line with what you've told us?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was exactly my question. This is a woman who was at the embassy in Zagreb at the very time of these events, and I'm simply asking her and she can corroborate, as we have put other witnesses in front of -- excuse me, other exhibits in front of other witnesses who can say, yes, I can corroborate, that was in fact the case. I simply asked her, based on her involvement at the embassy can she -- can she confirm to you Judges, as she sits here as a viva voce witness, that, yes, she knows that at this time there was tremendous international pressure being brought on Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And my point being, Mr. President, could have been very easily done this way and I hate to do Trial Advocacy 101 here in court, but it could have been, ma'am, at that point in time, what was the situation between Croatia, the state of Croatia, vis-a-vis the international community concerning the issue of refugees, and then the follow-up question. It's an open-ended way of doing it, as opposed to reading it and then saying, does this comport with what your knowledge is of the time. Keeping in mind now that the witness has been proofed by the Prosecution, shown all of these documents over the period a day or two, so really, it's a charade when you come to think of it, but the testimony is her memory. That's what the testimony is. Now, if he wants to get the document in, he can get it through other means but simply having a witness to vouch for it and vouch for what's in it is improper, unless he lays a foundation and the foundation would be in an open-ended fashion. Were you aware of what was happening in the international community vis-a-vis Croatia and refugees? Yes, no? If the answer is no, you move on. If the answer is yes, please explain, tell us, and then he can go on. Then if he wishes to read this, this portion, and say is this similar to what -- then she can say yes. But the way he's done it, he's tainted her, and now he's asking her to vouch for it. It's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. If I had been in your shoes, I would have proceeded the way Mr. Karnavas has outlined just now. I would have started with an open-ended question, and then depending on the answers given by the witness I would have asked her to confirm certain facts. You might have -- you were maybe trying to save time, but please try to be as professional as possible in order to avoid objections. When I put questions, I always start with an open-ended question, and depending on the answer I get I ask the witness to confirm what is being stated in a document shown to her. So what did you want to outline, to highlight here, because I'm lost now, Mr. Scott. What did you want to highlight? Did you want to highlight the pressures put to bear on the Croatian government because of the refugees, or was it the fact that this meeting, and I see that General Praljak was there, was it because during that meeting mention was made of the refugee problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a number of points -- there's several other points in the document that we haven't reached yet, but the point of the document, this first page, was simply the one that I put to the witness, yes, it might have been put differently, I wonder about the value of how much time we've wasted on the issue at this point, but simply this is someone who was an attache at the embassy and simply for her to confirm that that was the state of affairs at that time, and I think the witness should be prepared -- perhaps someone might have asked it differently. I think the witness should be allowed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Witness, I'm going to ask the question myself in order to avoid any problem. To your knowledge and considering the post that was yours at the embassy, and since you were closely -- worked closely with the ambassador, were you aware that the Croatian government was under pressure from the outside, including the European Union, with respect to what was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina and with respect to the arrival -- to the massive arrival of refugees, 600.000 of them in Croatia? Were you aware that the Croatian government was put under diplomatic pressure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was aware of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She was aware of it. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you -- I'm going to proceed in this order if I can --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. I think we're almost at the time for the next break but perhaps one or two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, around this time in the summer and early fall of 1993, what if anything did you know about the cooperation between Croats and Serbs in the area of Herzegovina and Dalmatia in this respect in -- concerning humanitarian matters or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: What I knew from my contacts with the refugees was that there was good cooperation between the Croat and Serb sides that was reflected in the following: Croatia provided fuel on trucks that Serbs took to their own front lines. I received daily information practically to that effect from refugees who were in the area of Split or, rather, the TTS terminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the TTS terminal?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: That's exactly what it was called, the TTS terminal. For me that was a place where a big humanitarian convoy was stopped and where it had to wait for six or seven months for its passage to be allowed through Croatia to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we can pick up there after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we -- before we just break, I just wanted to highlight some of the problems with this sort of testimony, because it's anecdotal. "From my contacts". We don't have names, we don't have places, we don't have dates, and yet we're supposed to cross-examine. I think it's a violation of our rights of confrontation when a witness comes in and says, it's just not hearsay, it's anecdotal, as I said. There is no particular individual that we know that we can then cross on. From my -- from my sources. And this has happened throughout. And I take it -- I know I'm dealing with professional Judges and I have the utmost confidence that they will see through this anecdotal testimony and realise that little, if no weight, should be given to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas. If I were in your shoes I would say -- on line 23 you just said -- page 23, page 71, received information and so on. So you could ask her, how did you know that the Croats were filling the tanks with oil for Serbs? Was that hearsay or what? And then according to the answer, it will give weight to it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is not for me to carry a burden. It is for the Prosecution to prove their case. And so when they come in and they have a witness that says, "From my sources, there was good cooperation between this group of people and that group of people," and then the Judges are going to give weight to it, I have to be concerned. It's not for me to try to figure out where she's getting this information. It's for the Prosecution to put it forward. And since they've asked that question I think a follow-up question should be at the return of the break, what about the cooperation between the Muslims and the Croats, the Muslims and the Serbs, and so on and so forth because I think this is the sort of question that should be asked on direct, not on cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We will have a 20-minute break and we will resume 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, before we continue on to another aspect of the -- another part of the transcript, let me just go back to your testimony before the break. We were talking about the cooperation between Croats and Serbs, and you were challenged about the foundation for this, but at lines 35 and 34 today, you said, "What I knew from my contacts with the refugees was there was good cooperation between the Croat and Serb sides that was reflected in the following: Croatia provided fuel trucks -- excuse me, fuel on trucks that Serbs took to their own front lines. I received daily information practically to that effect from refugees." Now, is that -- is that what you said, and is that one of the bases on which you indicated for the answer you gave? I'll ask you a question or two after that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said in my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you hear anything or did you receive any other information apart from that particular set of information, if you will, about oil on -- fuel on trucks? Did you receive any other information from refugees or through your embassy or other sources, and if you say, I'll ask you where or from who, about cooperation between the Croats and Serbs during this particular time, that is the summer and fall of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no other information reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on the transcript that you were looking at, we're still on Exhibit 5080, if I can ask you just to briefly go to page 6 of the English version, and I'll see if I can find the -- excuse me a moment. I believe on page -- if you can find -- the page numbers we'd normally have for some reason aren't on this particular document, but if you can find in the upper-left corner, I'm talking now about the Bosnian language version, up in the upper left corner 2/2/JG. If you see that. Otherwise, for the courtroom I'm referring to page 6 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I have the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And do you see that your name appears on that page?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it accurate that in fact indeed as you told us a few moments ago that as being reported here you were a member of that working group, as apparently President Tudjman knew? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask you then to go to page 16 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question, a follow-up question, please. President Tudjman is mentioning your name, Witness, and at a certain point in time he is going to ask the question, "Who is Zlatko Maric?" And Mate Boban answers, "I think Zlatko Maric is an advisor at the Islamic embassy." So why is Mate Boban mentioning the Islamic embassy? You're from the embassy of BiH, of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you have an opinion on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is that I have no information about the existence of a Islamic embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a colleague called Zlatko Maric that worked with you at the embassy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, there was a Mr. Zlatko Maric, and he did work as an advisor, a counsellor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can next ask you to go to page 17. The courtroom can go to page 17 of the English version of the transcript. We're still in document 5080, and to page - again what using the designations in the upper-left corner are 5/1/JG, or in the alternative is ERN number 01322671. That's the page in B/C/S. Madam, what I -- well, do you have that first of all?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, this is a portion of the transcript where Slobodan Praljak is talking, and starting with the part where he says: "They are ready and in a way they have reconciled themselves to the fact that the Muslims are on the Neretva River, let's say in Tasovcici, where they used to be. That is one thing. Another thing is the relations between the Croats and Serbs have improved, especially on a military plane, because our whole units depend on cooperation with the Serbs. In BH this agreement will aggravate that a lot. Therefore, Zepce, Kiseljak, and thus Vitez, the battalion below Konjic and Vares - it will now be difficult for us to provide them with supplies." And, madam, can you again -- is that consistent with the information you had at the time about the cooperation between Serbs and Croats about sending fuel to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was absolutely sure that Mr. Praljak was going to stand up. Mr. Praljak, I'm sure you want to take the floor, but could you tell us why? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The text wasn't correctly read out, and the translation is a poor one. It said, "They were ready, and in a sense they have come to terms with the fact that they are not on the Neretva." That's what it says in Croatian, and relates to the Serbs, not to the BH army. So could that be read out correctly and then the question be asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, did you take due note of Mr. Praljak's comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I heard his words, Your Honour, but I don't agree with him. I simply read exactly what's in the transcript. "Another thing is, the relations between the Croats and the Serbs have improved, especially on the military plane, because our whole units depend on cooperation with the Serbs ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, madam, is that consistent with what you knew, the reports you were receiving about cooperation between the Croats and the Serbs, including the sending of fuel to the front line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I think Mr. Murphy wanted to take the floor also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I would like to, Your Honour. If Mr. Scott could switch his microphone off. Your Honour, I think in fairness to Mr. Praljak, I understood his objection to be to the translation to a somewhat different passage of the transcript from the one that Mr. Scott just read out, I think the one in the preceding paragraph. Yes. And my colleague's suggesting, Your Honour, perhaps if the witness could read it out in the original language slowly so that the interpreters could interpret, perhaps we can then clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, please, could you read in your own language out loud the paragraph in question, and then the French and English interpreters will translate from your own language to -- to other languages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They are ready, and in a way they are reconciled to the fact that they are not on the Neretva River, but they will find it difficult to reconcile themselves with the fact that the Muslims are at the Neretva. For instance, in Tasovcici where they were. That's one thing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, on the transcript you now have the translation, the interpretation of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that we've gone through this exercise, Your Honour, but it has nothing to do whatsoever with my question. So we've spent time on it. But my question was about the next paragraph, and my question to the witness was:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that consistent -- I'll ask it for the third or fourth time now. Madam, is that consistent with the information that you had about cooperation between the Croats and the Serbs, including the shipment of fuel to the Serb front lines?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, that is completely in keeping with the information that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, this working group that was set up that involved you and, among others, Mr. Tadic and Mr. Zubak, did you in fact attend any meetings of this working group?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: We had several meetings, and the lowest number would be between 8 and 10, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges about the positions taken by Mr. Tadic at these meetings and if you found him to be someone who was constructive to deal with?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: In my opinion Mr. Tadic was someone who dealt primarily with creating problems and discussing matters that were not on the agenda of our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges what role Mr. Zubak played in the meetings that you attended of this working group?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: A completely passive role, except in several situations when I asked him for assistance to help us bring Mr. Tadic back to the topic that we had originally decided to meet to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the result of those efforts?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: The result was a protocol that was signed setting out the conditions to be fulfilled for the convoy which was stationed at the TTS for seven months would finally be allowed to move on to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'll come back to that topic a bit later of the convoy. Let me ask you if you can look at Exhibit P 00848, or in your binder it will just be 848. And in looking at that -- as you're looking for that, did you have any understanding of what body or organisation Mr. Tadic was part of in your dealings with him in these, I don't know, 8 or 10 meetings you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that at all. Now, I apologise, but the document under number 848, I don't seem to have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. 848, it would be at the very beginning, I believe. 848.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any information in your dealings with Mr. Tadic where his offices were located? Were you normally -- did you have any meetings with him at his office?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Never. I always kept notes about the meetings and the members of the working group, and next to their post it would just say -- or, rather, it would just say member of the working group and then the name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 18 of your statement, you make reference to something called the Office for Refugees from Siroki Brijeg. How did you come to know of an organisation or authority by that name?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: From the documents that I managed to obtain from the refugees or displaced persons in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you ever see Mr. Tadic's name on various of the documents that you saw that the refugees had, transit visas or permissions or any other documentation that they had in their possession?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: No, but in a few of the reports I saw that the signature on the document was illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Moving to paragraphs 91 and -- through 93 of your statement. You talk about the transfer of Muslim prisoners who had been held at Dretelj and their arrival on Korcula and Badija islands. And if I can ask you to look at 10055.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, I found the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By way of introduction to that document, can you tell us how did it come to your attention that these prisoners who had been released from Dretelj would be arriving in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I received that information from Ambassador Turkovic. And the information was confirmed by the Foreign Minister, Mr. Haris Silajdzic, because at that time he happened to be present. Actually, he came to the embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you now have Exhibit 10055, can you tell us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: This piece of information was sent out to the Foreign Minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it relates to the forthcoming disbanding of the Dretelj detainees or inmates, and the fact that it was planned that the former Dretelj inmates were going to be taken in temporarily on the island and the Gasinci centre before they went to third countries. No, I apologise. No. Just a moment. Until they went to third countries and until they were put up in the collection centres of Herceg-Bosnia. And it sets out the reasons for which this proposal was not taken on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, when you say to the island, you're now again talking about Obonjan?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: There was just one island, the island of Obonjan where the -- where a collective refugee centre existed as far as I know. It elaborates on the reasons for which we consider the proposal to be unacceptable. I don't know if you want me to address those reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: We informed our minister about the fact that both these centres, according to our terminology, were referred to as transit centres because of the specific conditions which prevailed in both those centres. What that meant, in fact, was that as soon as the refugees were taken in in one of the two centres, they sought ways and means of leaving Croatia as soon as possible and moving on to third countries. Now, the specific features under which they were accommodated in the collective centre at Obonjan was the very complex structure of the refugees and other BH citizens who spent time there. All of them were under constant supervision on the part of the special police forces of the Republic of Croatia, and refugees who had arrived there at the very beginning of the war and conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina were -- and who considered themselves to be old residents and thought they were to have certain benefits, thought they should have more benefits than the new arrivals, they were mixed up together. And also on the island you had former prisoners, some serious criminals, psychopaths, murderers who were there on the island waiting for the time to come to be returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina. So they were all mixed up together. And there were other people there whose status I never managed to learn, and I never knew what status they had. I never received either written or oral information either from the institutions of the Republic of Croatia or from the Gasinci centre director. And specifically there was a mother there with two small children who had been escorted by the Croatian police from their flat in Split and taken to the island. They were there. So their status was undetermined. And there was a group of people from Mostar, who had been expelled from Mostar, and they had no status either. So the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina thought this was serving time there, the fact they had been moved to the island, and refugees were there already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me discuss stop you there, madam, so we can move on. You've been mentioning that -- and in your letter, or in the letter -- or the report that's dated the 21st of September, Obonjan and Gasinski -- Gasinci, excuse me, but in fact you indicate in your statement that ultimately all these detainees were transported to Korcula and Badija islands; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: They were the ones from Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: That's where they ended up ultimately. Instead of Obonjan and Gasinci, their final destination was Korcula.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 96 of your statement that you spoke to both groups, asking if they were interested in going back to BiH since their families were there. They showed great interest in returning. Can you tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Most of them were very interested in returning to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and among the basic reasons for this that they gave for their return to Bosnia-Herzegovina was that their families had remained there in Herzegovina, and they feared for their safety, and they thought if they were able to go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina they'd be nearer their families and in a position to help them should the need arise. However, I should also like to say that among these former Dretelj inmates there were those who did wish to go on to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I can ask you, please, to go to Exhibit 10056. It should be the next -- hopefully it should be the very next document. And as soon as you have that, ma'am, can you look at that and tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes. This is a letter of the BH embassy in Zagreb, sent to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the working group for the protection of human rights in the territories under the control the BH army and the HVO, and it had to do with refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a letter that was written by the refugees department of the embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The second paragraph on the end of your letter, the penultimate paragraph, can you tell us -- you say: "All personal documents, money and valuables belonging to the detainees were confiscated in the Dretelj camp." What was the basis of your information for that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: On the basis of their written and oral statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to the next document, 10057.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what is that, please?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Again, information sent to BH institutions, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to the working group, established on the basis of the Izetbegovic-Tudjman agreement and the Directorate for Displaced Persons and Refugees. This is information about negotiations conducted on the basis of the joint declaration of the 14th of September. This information pertains to the exchange of prisoners -- or, rather, the position of the Directorate for Refugees and Displaced Persons and the department for refugees of the BH embassy that released detainees should not be taken out of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia. The position was that these detainees should be sent to the Tuzla region because that region at that point in time did have the capacity to take these people in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Tuzla at that time was a part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was under the control of the Sarajevo government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: It was part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were detainees that were from Dretelj who were released from Dretelj and then sent to Croatia, were they then allowed to be relocated to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: On our part we were looking at the possibility of transferring them to Tuzla, which meant providing for their security as they pass through Herzegovina on route to their final destination, namely Tuzla. The negotiators did not manage to secure guarantees from the HVO that these former detainees from Dretelj could safely go through this territory. Therefore, we, on our part, could not make it possible for them to have their wish come true, namely to go back to Bosnia. So that is why they did not do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 93 of your statement you talk about the conditions of some of the men who were released from Dretelj. You say: "I was appalled --" paragraph 93.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "I was appalled when I saw the 'better-off cases'. Many of them were walking dead people. They were exhausted. I remember one of them was wounded in the leg because he was shot by one of the guards in the prison. One had a broken leg, and most of them were suffering with diarrhoea and itching." Did you take any steps to get medical treatment or medical inspections for the people, these men who had been released from Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Immediately upon returning from this visit I asked the ambassador to mobilise a team of doctors who would go to Badija and visit both groups. Part of them were in Badija, and another part were at the Alfir hotel in Korcula. I wanted our doctors to establish the condition of the former detainees so that we could take the steps we could in view of the fact that we were guests in that country in order to provide at least basic medical care to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you in this regard come to know of or involve a doctor by the name of Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: In addition to others, Dr. Aida Kapetanovic was in this group, who together with the others carried out this task and submitted a written report to the embassy, or rather the department for refugees as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn to Exhibit 10058.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: This is the report of Dr. Aida Kapetanovic on her visit to the island of Badija, and her encounter with 300 former detainees. In this document, Dr. Kapetanovic also states certain facts that have to do with the former detainees of Dretelj and how thin they had become, how long they were detained, what kind of health problems they had. At any rate, the doctor confirmed our first findings. I mean, we from the department of refugees are not medical personnel ourselves, but we did recognise these things. Dr. Aida also confirmed some of the other findings that had to do with the living conditions in Badija. She confirmed that they did not have proper medical care, and then on the basis of this report we sent a document to international and other humanitarian organisations present in the Republic of Croatia saying that medicaments and other elementary supplies were needed for these former detainees. We kindly asked them to provide what was necessary for these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, were you ever able or successful, not just you personally of course but your embassy and the government, to succeed in having these prisoners released anywhere other than to third countries? For the most part. I realise there may have been a few exceptions, but what happened to most of the people who were released or transferred from Dretelj to Korcula and Badija?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge or as far as I know, all of them had to leave both Badija and the Alfir hotel because they were actually staying there only on a temporary basis. When I visited Badija and the island of Korcula the second time I saw representatives of the UNHCR there, and I believe that they actually took care of about 90 per cent of the former detainees, that they went to third countries, that is. In addition to the UNHCR, there were other organisations that offered such services and facilitated their transfer to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question, Witness, one follow-up question. I read the report prepared by Dr. Kapetanovic with great interest, and in this report we see that these people were there momentarily, had one concern; they wanted to have a passport from their own country, because when they arrived there they were not in possession of passports or IDs. Since they were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and since you were a member of that embassy, why did the authorities of your country, of the consular authority, why did they not provide these people with passports? What was the problem? Because the -- these people were nationals of your country, and you were working at the embassy. Why didn't you deliver or issue passports to these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was our custom to organise consular days in all big refugee centres. First, they were organised on a monthly basis and after that every month and a half or two. So there were technical problems -- there weren't, rather, any technical problems in having consular staff getting to Badija or Korcula. However, we could not get consent to go and contact the former detainees of Dretelj in that way, and that is the only reason why they could not get our passports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise, you could have issued passports to them without any problem; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could have done that without any problem whatsoever. We already had experience on that score. We organised photograph-taking of BH citizens and also the issuing of passports at particular refugee centres, but beforehand we always had the prior consent of Croatian institutions to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not take into account people coming from Dretelj and sent to these two islands. Let's talk about the other people, those who were located on the other island where you yourself went for a visit. Those people on the other island, did you issue passports to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that you're referring to the group of citizens who were expelled from Mostar. We did not issue passports to that group either for a simple reason, because that group only had permission to stay in Croatia for a given number of hours in transit, but we issued collective passports to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why not issue individual passports to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it was difficult for us to see to their relocation from a technical point of view. We received information from the embassy of the Republic of Turkey that Turkey was prepared to take in about 2.000 citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were not able to stay in the republic of Croatia. We had a very short deadline to prepare this group for travel, and that is the reason why we issued a collective passport, because we knew that they would be collectively put up in Turkey, and that later on there they would have the opportunity of receiving individual passports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about those who did not wish to go to Turkey, because obviously in that group you had people who did not wish to go to third countries; they wanted to go home. Why not issue individual passports to these people and then it was up to them to try and cross check-points if they wanted to do so, because they were free to move around, although the local authorities, of course, were in a position to control them. But they were -- they had freedom of movement. Why didn't you at the embassy issue individual passports to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite literally there was no request of that nature. All of them left after they signed a document that they would leave all their properties and that they were leaving the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they would go to third countries, and that they would never return to Bosnia-Herzegovina again. That is to say that no one tried to return on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am sorry, I apologise to my colleague. This is not an answer to the question. This document clearly shows that they did want passports. We have on page 2 of the English version, at the bottom, it says: "The UNHCR is bringing pressure to bear that they have to sign up for going to third countries."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that we do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, I would like to draw your attention to the last paragraph where the doctor said they were given refugee status, because the witness said a few minutes ago that, like the previous group, this group was there only in transit and that they could stay only for a few hours whereas here it says they could have stayed as refugees with that status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had noted that as well. Witness, the third line before the end, Dr. Kapetanovic seems to be saying that these people had obtained refugee status. She might be mistaken, of course, but that's what we read here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really did not see this earlier on either. I did not have such information, and so far I had not noticed that this was included in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Judges will draw the necessary conclusions. Mr. Scott, we have 10 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, just so the record is clear because some people may not be clear with the terminology, and for the record, when you say "collective passport," what is a collective passport, and how does one prepare such a document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: This is a document that is prepared for group travel. It is issued in the name and -- in the name and surnames of all the persons on a given -- in a given group, and their names and surnames are provided, and also individual photographs are provided for each and every member of the group. So these were the travel documents that we were in a position to issue in a very short period of time. I even remember a situation when we were doing that at the Split airport, issuing these collective passports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you also made reference in the last few minutes to a document that these people were required to sign about giving over their property and promising never to return to, you said, Bosnia-Herzegovina. And at what point in this series of steps or events were they required to sign that document, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: At that time they were still in Dretelj, and those were the conditions on which they could have been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall -- when you say never to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it -- if you remember, was the promise that they would never return to Bosnia-Herzegovina or that they would never return to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: In our communication we used the term "Bosnia-Herzegovina." However, my precise understanding was that it was the territory not under the control of the BH army but, rather, of the HVO -- or, rather, the territory under the control of the Serb forces was not safe for their return at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, but I think that the witness is saying, "In our conversation they said Bosnia-Herzegovina." Can she explain how come she had this interpretation that it is not territory that was under the control of the HVO and the army of Republika Srpska? There is some confusion there now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally was never confused at any point in time. When I was in contact with the former detainees of Dretelj, it was quite clear to me, as it is today, that they did not have the motive, wish, or courage to return to that area of Herzegovina then. This explains my motive. When we mention the country, officially it was Bosnia-Herzegovina. In a narrower sense, if what was being referred to was the territory where they themselves did not feel they could move about safely, these were territories that were not under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, theoretically, could a refugee -- refugee in one of these camps in Croatia, could this refugee theoretically have gone not to Herzegovina but to a -- to a town under the control of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because by land one had to go through the territory of Herceg-Bosna, rather, territory under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, before we go on to another topic and then we'll come back to this issue counsel has raised about the status of refugees, but in paragraphs 98 and 99 of your statement you make reference to the fact that you actually had contact with some of these people later. Not at this particular moment in 1993, but later on. And did you in fact come into contact with people who were at that time trying to return, then, from these third countries back to their homes in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. These were people who were out in Spain, and they often contacted my department by telephone and spoke to me personally as well. I also had an encounter with two former detainees of Dretelj at the airport in Zagreb. I was waiting for an UNHCR flight from Zagreb to Sarajevo, and they had just arrived from Spain. We met up, and I received information from them then that they were expecting permission to go back to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in this connection can I ask you to look at Exhibit 10067.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: It's a letter of the BH embassy in Croatia, the department for refugees, pertaining to the return of former detainees to RBiH. The letter is sent to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the RBiH. Letters written by former Dretelj detainees were attached to this letter. They were calling from Denmark and Spain. Actually, in their own letters they were asking the embassy for help, because they did not have any information about their family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps we can finish on this question. Given -- this is in -- this is the 17th of May, 1994. Given the number of issues that your embassy was dealing with around that time, why did you find it noteworthy to send a report on this topic to your superiors in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK
utterances.text: Because my department did not cover problems related to refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were in Spain, Denmark, and third countries. I thought that there were institutions and embassies that could and should deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might suggest that that would be a good place to stop for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Scott. Let me inform you that you've used up two hours and seven minutes. It's almost 7.00 p.m. Witness, you've given the solemn declaration. That is to say that you're not supposed to have contacts with anyone from the Defence or the Prosecution. As you know, we'll continue your testimony tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m. I wish you a very pleasant evening, and I'll see you all tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
